strengths: The GESPI framework is elegantly simple and genuinely general: it wraps around any base inference procedure satisfying a monotone risk condition (Eq. 5), with instances given for conformal prediction, conformal risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, outlier detection, and multiple testing (FWER). The unified decision-theoretic formulation (Section 3.4, Condition F.1) is clean and covers all examples in Table 1/3.

The guarantees are distribution-free and finite-sample: Theorem 3.2 gives risk <= alpha + min(epsilon, c * d_TV) adapting continuously to synthetic data quality, and Theorem 3.3 gives a deterministic sandwich between Alg_alpha and Alg_{alpha+epsilon}. The proofs are correct and self-contained.

Proposition E.1 is a valuable conceptual contribution: it shows that uniformly controlling risk over all synthetic distributions Q forces one to (essentially) ignore the synthetic data, which honestly clarifies why the alpha+epsilon guardrail target is the right one and positions the paper's ambition appropriately.

Experiments are broad and relevant to modern practice: AlphaFold2 risk control on CASP-14 with MSA-derived synthetic data, LLM win-rate testing on AIME25 (with a clever shuffled-response null for Type I error estimation), conformal outlier detection with contaminated reference sets, and a mechanistic interpretability test on CLIP. The controlled simulation study (Section C.1, Figures 6-10) systematically ablates rho_synt, epsilon, n, N, and alpha, and empirically confirms both power gains and error control at alpha+epsilon.

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and honest about limitations (the discussion acknowledges that power gains depend on synthetic data quality; related work, especially SPI by Bashari et al. 2025, is transparently credited and the differences articulated).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. The core construction—run the base method on pooled data at alpha, on real data at alpha+epsilon, and combine via AND/OR—is a straightforward guardrail/monotone-aggregation trick, and the main theorems follow from a few lines of TV-distance bounding (proofs in Section I are elementary). Relative to SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a), which the paper explicitly identifies as the direct inspiration, the contribution is primarily a reformulation and generalization rather than a new mechanism; the ε-inflated guarantee is also essentially the same kind of trade-off SPI provides.

The price of the guardrail is a real cost that deserves deeper discussion: the guaranteed level is alpha + epsilon, not alpha, so the method can be strictly less conservative in error control than the base method even when synthetic data are useless; how to choose epsilon adaptively or data-dependently is not addressed (noted only as future work).

The general bound in Theorem 3.2 involves the instance-specific TV quantity d_{f,Alg}(P,Q), which is generally not estimable or interpretable; the sharpest results (Theorem H.1, H.3) are confined to special cases with strong assumptions (e.g., continuous score distributions), so the practical interpretability of the theory varies across applications.

Some experimental choices feel ad hoc: in the protein experiment the synthetic 'labels' are PAE-based proxies with an ad hoc filtering rule (discard proteins with >50% residues above 3Å under the proxy), which makes it hard to assess how results depend on that heuristic; the trimming of the contaminated reference set by an Isolation Forest in Section 4.3 similarly introduces an uncontrolled heuristic step into the pipeline.

Several application details (e.g., the ViT interpretability case study) mainly illustrate that valid tests can be run with synthetic data, but provide little evidence the gains are substantial relative to simply collecting a modest amount of additional real data; a cost/benefit comparison against real-data baselines would strengthen the significance claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: how to safely leverage synthetic data in statistical inference without distributional assumptions on the synthetic data.

The proposed GESPI wrapper is genuinely general: it applies to conformal prediction, conformal risk control, hypothesis testing, outlier detection, and multiple testing without modifying the base procedure, which is an attractive plug-and-play design.

The guarantees are clean, finite-sample, and distribution-free: worst-case error control at α+ε via the guardrail (Theorem 3.2/3.3), with tighter control degrading gracefully with the TV-distance between real and synthetic distributions.

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is a nice touch, clarifying that uniform control at level α over all synthetic distributions essentially reduces to ignoring the synthetic data, thereby justifying the relaxed target.

The empirical evaluation is broad and creative, spanning AlphaFold protein structure prediction with conformal risk control, LLM win-rate testing on AIME25/OlympiadBench, contaminated reference sets for outlier detection, and a mechanistic interpretability test on CLIP, with ablations on ε, sample sizes, and synthetic data quality.
Experimental details are thorough (Appendix B), and the paper is honest that power gains depend on synthetic data quality.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution is elementary. Theorem 3.2 follows from the observation that the loss of a meet (∧) of two procedures is bounded by the minimum of their losses, combined with a standard TV bound; the proof in Section I.2 is a few lines. The guardrail trick—combining procedures at levels α and α+ε—is a well-known construction, and the paper does not position its contribution against this line of work convincingly.

Novelty relative to the closest prior work (SPI, Bashari et al., 2025a) is limited. The paper itself frames GESPI as a 'reformulation' of SPI that treats conformal prediction as a black box rather than modifying score transportation; this is an incremental generalization, and the main theorems do not substantially deepen the theory beyond what such a reformulation trivially enables.

The practical guarantee is only at level α+ε in the worst case, and ε must be fixed a priori with no principled guidance. In applications where α itself is the target (e.g., FWER control at 15% with ε=10% in Section 4.3), the worst-case guarantee may be too loose to be scientifically meaningful.

Some experimental constructions weaken the claimed 'synthetic data' framing. In Section 4.1, the 'synthetic' data are AlphaFold Database predictions for MSA sequences with PAE-based error proxies, and proteins are filtered using the proxy error (discarding those with >50% residues above 3Å); this filtering uses distributional knowledge that is not fully distribution-free in spirit, and the resulting conclusions depend on these choices.

The quantitative evidence is largely empirical and coarse: e.g., the protein results average over 38 proteins with only 10 real ones per trial, and the LLM experiment uses n=15 real problems; the observed gains, while consistent, are modest and the paper offers little analysis of when the guardrail is actually active.

The main text is somewhat thin on the general framework; key material (formal conditions, two-sided guardrails, application-specific theorems, multiple testing) is deferred to appendices, and the core message of Section 3.4 reduces to one formula (6) plus a simple theorem.

Comparison baselines are limited: the paper compares against OnlyReal and the invalid OnlySynth, but not against other principled ways of combining real and auxiliary data under distribution shift (e.g., prediction-powered inference variants or weighting-based approaches), making it hard to assess the practical advantage of the guardrail design.

strengths: The core idea is simple, general, and well-executed: GESPI wraps any base inference procedure by taking the meet of a synthetic-powered run at level alpha (on pooled data) and a guardrail run at level alpha+epsilon (on real data only), yielding a distribution-free, finite-sample risk bound (alpha + min{epsilon, c*TV}) that holds for arbitrary synthetic data quality without any distributional assumptions on Q.

The theoretical treatment is clean and complete: Condition F.1 is mild and verified for standard inference problems; Theorem 3.2 gives the adaptive risk bound, Theorem 3.3/F.2 gives a deterministic sandwich guarantee ensuring the wrapped procedure never underperforms the base method and never exceeds the guardrail; Proposition E.1 provides an impossibility result that meaningfully justifies the alpha+epsilon target as the right notion of 'worst-case safety', which elevates the paper beyond a simple construction.

The framework is instantiated across a broad range of tasks (conformal prediction and risk control, one-sided hypothesis testing, FWER/k-FWER multiple testing, outlier detection with contaminated reference sets) with application-specific sharper bounds (e.g., Theorem H.1 for conformal prediction with order-statistic TV distance).

Experiments are diverse, realistic, and convincing: protein structure prediction with AlphaFold2 (using MSAs as synthetic data - a clever and practically motivated construction), LLM win-rate testing on AIME25 with OlympiadBench as non-i.i.d. synthetic data, outlier detection on benchmark tabular datasets, and a ViT mechanistic interpretability application. Controlled simulations systematically isolate the effects of synthetic-data quality, epsilon, alpha, and sample sizes, and consistently confirm the theory (GESPI's Type I error stays below alpha+epsilon, power exceeds OnlyReal when synthetic data is informative).

Reproducibility is good: experimental details are thorough (model configurations, prompts, data splits, trial counts, verification pipelines), and the methods are simple to implement. Limitations (dependence of power gain on synthetic data quality) are honestly stated.
weaknesses: The central construction is conceptually straightforward - intersect a synthetic-powered output with a guardrail output, then apply a standard TV-distance argument. The main theorem's proof is only a few lines, and the framework is best viewed as a black-box reformulation/generalization of Synthetic-Powered Predictive Inference (Bashari et al., 2025) rather than a fundamentally new technical mechanism. Readers seeking deep technical novelty may find the contribution modest.

The epsilon slack is always paid in the worst-case guarantee, and the theory offers no guidance on choosing epsilon; an overly large epsilon weakens validity while a small one limits the guardrail's power benefit. The bound's dependence on the TV term d_{f,Alg}(P,Q), which can be large in practice, means the adaptive part of the guarantee may be loose outside well-behaved settings.

Some real-data experiments are small in scale (e.g., n=10 CASP-14 proteins, n=15 AIME25 questions with two model comparisons), so empirical power estimates carry nontrivial variance; the paper mitigates this with repeated trials, but the practical gains in these specific applications are demonstrated on a limited set of examples.

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) shows uniform control over all synthetic distributions is dominated by ignoring synthetic data, but the paper stops short of characterizing when GESPI is minimax-optimal or how close it gets to the best achievable power given n real and N synthetic samples.

Discussion of potential double-dipping or data-dependent synthetic-data selection (Remark F.4 only partially addresses this) is brief; a deeper treatment of adaptive/learned synthetic data curation, acknowledged as future work, would strengthen the practical story.

strengths: The GESPI framework is clean and general: wrapping any risk-controlling inference procedure with three calls (base, guardrail at alpha+epsilon, synthetic-powered) yields a simple, distribution-free construction applicable to conformal prediction, risk control, hypothesis testing, and multiple testing, all covered by one decision-theoretic formulation (Condition F.1, Eq. 5-6).

Theoretical results are correct and appropriately scoped: Theorem 3.3 gives an interpretable TV-distance-based risk bound that interpolates between alpha and alpha+epsilon as synthetic quality varies; Theorem 3.4/F.2 guarantee the two-sided guardrail never underperforms the base method; Proposition E.1 provides a useful impossibility result motivating the epsilon relaxation; Section H gives tighter task-specific bounds (e.g., Theorem H.1 for conformal prediction).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and well-designed: ImageNet conformal prediction with genuinely low-quality FLUX synthetic data (OnlySynth at ~60% coverage), AlphaFold/CASP-14 risk control with a creative MSA-based synthetic data construction, outlier detection with contaminated reference sets, LLM win-rate testing with a proper null via shuffled responses, and a ViT interpretability case study. Controlled simulations (Figures S1-S5) systematically study sensitivity to epsilon, synthetic quality, and sample sizes.

The paper is honest that baselines like OnlySynth and Synth+Real lack guarantees and includes them only to characterize synthetic data quality; an honest limitations paragraph in the Discussion acknowledges that gains depend on synthetic data quality.
Software for reproduction is referenced, and experimental details (models, prompts, datasets, thresholds) are documented thoroughly in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core construction is conceptually simple - aggregate the base algorithm's outputs at levels alpha and alpha+epsilon via meet/join operations - and the main theoretical results follow fairly directly from monotonicity of the loss plus TV-distance continuity. The novelty relative to SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a) is primarily generality (black-box treatment of the base procedure and extension beyond conformal prediction) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which may limit the contribution's depth for a main-track venue.

The worst-case guarantee is always alpha+epsilon even when synthetic data are perfect: the guaranteed bound never improves below the guardrail level, so a practitioner always 'pays' epsilon relative to the nominal level. The paper does not deeply address how to choose epsilon in practice, and the trade-off between the epsilon cost and potential utility gains is left to the user with limited guidance.

Some empirical settings are thin: the LLM comparison experiments use only n=15 real problems (a subset of the 30 in AIME25), and in several applications (C.4, C.7) GESPI's power is essentially indistinguishable from the trivial Guardrail baseline, so the demonstrated advantage over simply running the base test at level alpha+epsilon is modest in those cases. The variance-reduction benefit (Section C.2.1) requires a somewhat artificial alignment of mean empirical coverage to interpret.

The dependence of the key quantity d_t,Alg(P,Q) on the algorithm and the number of synthetic samples is not characterized; the bound in Theorem 3.3 is conservative and the paper provides no finite-sample guidance on how large N must be for the synthetic-powered term to help.

The limitations discussion is brief; topics such as computational cost of running the base procedure three times, behavior under non-monotone or non-lattice action spaces, and dependence assumptions between real and synthetic data generation processes (e.g., LLM-generated math problems resembling test items) deserve more careful treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely question: how to exploit abundant synthetic/auxiliary data for statistical inference while retaining rigorous, distribution-free error guarantees without any assumptions on the synthetic distribution.

The framework is clean and genuinely general: it treats the base inference procedure as a black box and requires only a partially ordered action space with a monotone, bounded loss (Condition F.1), covering conformal prediction, conformal risk control, single and multiple hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals in a unified way.

The theory is coherent and honest about what is achievable: Theorem 3.3 gives a TV-distance-controlled risk bound, Theorem 3.4 guarantees the two-sided procedure is sandwiched between the base method and the guardrail (so utility never degrades), and Proposition E.1 is a nice impossibility result showing that uniform control at level α over all synthetic distributions would essentially make the synthetic data useless—thereby justifying the ε 'admission cost' design.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad (ImageNet conformal prediction, AlphaFold2 conformal risk control with creatively constructed MSA-based synthetic data, conformal outlier detection with FWER control, LLM win-rate testing on AIME25, ViT mechanistic interpretability), with controlled simulations that isolate the effects of ε, sample sizes, and synthetic-data quality.

The paper is transparent about baselines that lack guarantees (OnlySynth, Synth+Real) and about when comparisons are only illustrative; code availability is stated and experimental details (Section B) are fairly thorough, supporting reproducibility.
Limitations are discussed candidly (power gain depends on synthetic quality), and the discussion does not overstate the contribution.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is thin: GESPI is essentially a union/intersection (OR/AND) aggregation of three runs of an existing procedure at levels α, α+ε on real data and α on pooled data. The main proofs (I.2, I.4) are short manipulations of monotonicity plus a TV bound; the technical depth resides mostly in specialized results (e.g., Theorem H.1), and the generalization beyond SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a) is an incremental 'wrapper' extension rather than a new mechanism.

The theoretical guarantees are conservative and somewhat loose: the risk bound α + min{ε, c·d_TV} involves a crude TV term, and in Theorem F.2 an additional slack term cτ appears even under perfect synthetic data (P=Q), reflecting bias introduced by the guardrails themselves. The practically relevant utility gain (variance/power improvement) is largely asserted empirically rather than characterized theoretically in general.

The value proposition of the ε cost is debatable: in the worst case the user permanently 'pays' ε in error level relative to the base method with no benefit, and the paper offers no principled guidance for choosing ε beyond it being user-specified; adaptivity to synthetic quality is observed empirically but not designed.

Some experiments have limited statistical resolution or scope: e.g., the protein experiment uses only 10 real proteins out of 38, results are averaged over just 10 repeats, and the LLM win-rate study uses n=15 real questions; several claims (e.g., variance reduction benefits) rest on selected classes or illustrative comparisons the authors themselves note are not feasible in practice (Figure 5 ROC, Figure 7 alignment by empirical coverage).

Presentation has rough edges: footnote-level clarification is needed for the nesting in Eq. (1), the multiple-testing treatment is deferred almost entirely to the appendix (Sections D, G, H), and the main text leaves important condition-checking (monotonicity of base algorithms, Table S2) to the reader.

The related work positioning, while extensive (Section A), acknowledges close neighbors in prediction-powered inference and prior-data combination; a sharper articulation of why those lines cannot be adapted to give the same distribution-free guarantee would strengthen the case for the framework's necessity.

strengths: The GESPI framework is simple, general, and principled: wrapping any error-controlling inference procedure with a base/guardrail/pooled aggregation yields distribution-free risk control (Theorem 3.3) with no assumptions on the synthetic data distribution, plus a deterministic utility sandwich guarantee (Theorem 3.4). The framework cleanly covers conformal prediction, risk control, single and multiple hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals via the partial-order action space abstraction (Condition F.1).

The impossibility result (Proposition E.1) is a valuable conceptual contribution: it shows that requiring level-α control uniformly over all synthetic distributions essentially forces ignoring the synthetic data, thereby justifying the ε-relaxed target as the 'cost' of using synthetic data.

Experiments are broad and well-designed: ImageNet conformal prediction, AlphaFold/AlphaFold2 conformal risk control with a creative reuse of MSAs as synthetic data, outlier detection (single and multiple testing), LLM win-rate testing on AIME25 with OlympiadBench as synthetic data, and ViT interpretability. The controlled simulations (Figures S1–S5) systematically isolate the effects of synthetic quality, ε, n, N, and α. The inclusion of OnlySynth/Synth+Real baselines clearly illustrates what happens when synthetic data are naively trusted.

The paper validates the guarantees empirically (error rates never exceed α+ε) and demonstrates power/variance gains when synthetic data are useful, and graceful degradation to the base method when they are not. Software is released, experimental details are thorough, and the limitations discussion is honest (power depends on synthetic quality; ε trade-off).

The two-sided guardrail (Theorem F.2) with refined bounds (Section H, e.g., Theorem H.1 with order-statistic TV bounds for conformal prediction) shows the framework supports tighter, application-specific guarantees beyond the generic TV bound.
weaknesses: Core methodological novelty is modest. The idea of aggregating a synthetic-data-based procedure with a real-data-based procedure at a relaxed level to retain validity is a natural construction, and the main theorems follow from short monotonicity/TV arguments. The paper is best viewed as a careful generalization of SPI (Bashari et al., 2025a) from conformal prediction to a general decision-theoretic wrapper; the delta over that prior work, while real (pooled-data usage, black-box treatment), is incremental.

The guarantees are inherently conservative: the worst-case risk is α+ε and utility is bounded by the guardrail, so the method pays ε even when synthetic data quality is bad, and gains nothing guaranteed beyond the base method unless the synthetic data are close to real. The bound in Theorem 3.3 involves the TV distance of the full pooled-data output distribution, which can be vacuous in practice; the refined per-application bounds mitigate this but only for specific cases.

There is no principled guidance for choosing ε: it is described as a user-specified 'admission cost' and the ablations show performance varies substantially with ε, but the paper offers no data-driven selection procedure (which, admittedly, would be difficult without violating the guarantees).

Some experimental evidence is thin relative to the breadth of claims: the protein experiment uses only n=10 real proteins out of 38 with 10 repetitions; the LLM experiments use n=15 AIME25 questions with a validation approach (shuffled answers) that is only an approximate null; class-conditional coverage is evaluated per class with n=15 real images, where the reported gains are largely variance reduction rather than a shift in mean performance.

The multiple testing extension is given only at a high level in the main text (Section 3.3) with details deferred to the appendix, and the FWER experiments require a trimming heuristic whose interaction with the guarantees deserves more discussion (trimming uses the model scores on the contaminated set, and the paper does not fully characterize how the 'pseudo-inlier' quality affects the bound).
